Chapter 3: OxyContin and the Making of a Crisis.
Pain. It's something we've all felt, right? For some folks, though, pain isn't just a passing thing—it shapes every single day, every choice.
Back in the 1990s, doctors started looking at pain in a new way. Instead of just asking about it, they were told to treat pain like a vital sign—something you needed to attack head-on. That shift opened the door for a whole new kind of medicine.
Now, Purdue Pharma, which had grown out of Purdue Frederick, saw a huge opportunity here. The Sackler family believed they could make a painkiller that was both strong and safe. Their big idea? OxyContin—a time-release version of oxycodone. The pitch sounded convincing: if the drug released slowly, you’d get long-lasting relief, but without the risk of addiction.
The launch of OxyContin? Honestly, it was marketing genius. Purdue's sales team was trained to tell doctors that OxyContin was less addictive than other opioids, all thanks to its special time-release formula. They handed out free samples, hosted educational seminars, even offered little perks to doctors who wrote the prescriptions. Everywhere you looked, the message was clear—OxyContin was a breakthrough, a safe answer for anyone living with chronic pain.
Doctors were already under pressure to treat pain more seriously, so they jumped on board. Prescriptions took off. People who’d been suffering for years finally found some relief. For a while, it really did seem like a miracle cure.
But underneath all that hope, trouble was starting to bubble up. Some patients began showing signs of addiction. Others figured out they could crush the pills to get a quicker, more intense high. Reports of abuse and overdoses started to surface. Still, Purdue insisted the risks were tiny. They said addiction was rare—and only happened with a handful of so-called “abusers” who didn’t take the drug as directed.
Even inside Purdue, there were red flags. Some employees worried that the marketing claims were overblown, that the company was looking the other way as evidence of abuse piled up. But the pressure to keep those sales numbers climbing was just too strong. And anyone who raised concerns? They usually got ignored or pushed aside.
Meanwhile, the damage outside was impossible to miss. All across the country, communities started seeing more addiction, more overdoses, and more deaths. Families were torn apart. Quiet small towns became places of heartbreak and loss. The opioid crisis had begun—and so much of it traced back to the aggressive push behind OxyContin.
Most people had no idea who was really behind it all. The Sackler name still stood for art, education, and healing. Nobody connected their wealth to the growing wave of tragedy. That link was carefully hidden away, protected by layers of secrecy and denial.
In the end, it became clear—the opioid epidemic wasn’t some random disaster. It was the outcome of conscious decisions. Choices made in boardrooms and marketing meetings, far from the lives that would be shattered as a result.
